findings.title: do_exec passes the raw argc to init_pcb_stack while init_user_stack builds the array from a clamped argc
findings.detail:
init_user_stack() (lines 147-152) sanitises its *local* copy of argc (`argc = 0` when `argc < 0 || argv == NULL`, clamp to MAX_EXEC_ARGC = 16) and builds a NULL-terminated array of exactly that many entries. do_exec() then hands the *unsanitised* caller value to init_pcb_stack at line 248-249, so a0 (argc) and the array a1 points at disagree.

Failure scenario A: a user task calls `sys_exec("rw", 20, argv20, AUTO_CLEANUP_ON_EXIT)`. init_user_stack writes 16 pointers + a NULL at sp; init_pcb_stack sets a0 = 20. The child's `for (i = 1; i < argc; i++) atol(argv[i])` reads argv[16] = NULL and argv[17..19] from sp+136, which is the first bytes of the topmost argument string reinterpreted as pointers. atol() then dereferences that garbage; if it lands >= 2^38 handle_page_fault() forwards to handle_other() -> assert(0), panicking the whole kernel (global lock, both harts).

Failure scenario B: `sys_exec("rw", 2, NULL, ...)`. init_user_stack sets its argc to 0 and emits a single NULL slot at 0xf0000fff8, but a0 = 2. The child reads argv[1] at 0xf00010000, which is one byte past the top of the mapped stack frame - a fresh demand-paged zero page - then dereferences the resulting NULL. Fix: return/propagate the clamped argc from init_user_stack and use it for regs[10].

findings.title: init_user_stack can write past the single user stack frame into the physically preceding frame
findings.detail:
init_user_stack() maps exactly one page (line 138) and then copies argv into it with no check that `sp` stays >= top_va - PAGE_SIZE. The only limit is MAX_EXEC_ARGC = 16 entries; individual string lengths come from strlen() on caller-controlled pointers and are unbounded. The page holds at most 4096 - 8*(argc+1) bytes of strings (3960 for argc=16).

Failure scenario: `sys_exec("rw", 16, argv, ...)` with 16 arguments of ~300 bytes each (4800 bytes). At line 157-158 `sp` walks below 0xf0000f000, so STACK_KVA(sp) walks below the frame base and memcpy writes ~840 bytes into the *physically preceding* frame through the kernel direct map (pa2kva). That frame is an unrelated live process's page - silent cross-process corruption with no fault, since the kernel window maps all of 0x50000000-0x60000000 R/W. If the stack frame handed out happens to be the first user frame (pa 0x51000000 == USER_MEM_BEGIN), the overflow lands at 0x50fff000, inside the kernel heap region (KERNEL_MEM_BEGIN..KERNEL_MEM_END).

This is also reachable indirectly from the shipped shell: test_shell.c prints "Too many arguments!" but keeps parsing, so with 11+ words `sys_exec(argv[1], 10, _argv, ...)` is issued while `_argv` only has MAX_ARGC-1 = 9 entries; init_user_stack reads _argv[9]/_argv[10] off the end of the shell's frame and strlen()s whatever garbage pointer it finds, which can yield a length far larger than a page. The kernel must clamp the total to the frame it allocated regardless of what the caller passes.

findings.title: do_exec dereferences user pointers that may not be resident, and a kernel-mode page fault self-deadlocks on the non-recursive kernel lock
findings.detail:
do_exec() enables SUM (line 189) and then dereferences `file_name` (get_elf_file -> strcmp) and `argv[i]` / `*argv[i]` (lines 156-158) with no residency guarantee. With P4's demand paging plus swapping, those user pages can be absent.

Why the fault is fatal rather than serviced: while in a syscall, sscratch holds the pcb (non-zero), so a fault taken in S-mode enters exception_handler_entry, takes the `from_user` branch (`bnez tp`), overwrites PCB_USER_SP(tp) with the kernel sp, and then does `call lock_kernel`. lock_kernel is a plain non-recursive spinlock (kernel/locking/lock.c spin_lock_try_acquire) already held by this hart since the outer trap - the hart spins forever, and because the lock is global the other hart wedges at its next trap. The machine hangs with no diagnostic.

Concrete triggers: (1) a user task calling `sys_exec("rw", 1, (char**)0x20000000, ...)` with an address it has never touched; (2) ordering inside do_exec itself - init_page_table()/load_elf() run *before* the arguments are read (lines 219-246), and alloc_user_page() can call selete_page()/write_to_sd() which may evict the caller's own stack page holding argv, so the subsequent strlen(argv[i]) faults on a page do_exec just swapped out. Copying file_name and the argv strings into kernel memory before any allocation, and validating the pointers, avoids both. (Not reachable with the shipped shell on the default 208 MB user pool, where swapping never happens - hence minor - but it is latent whenever memory pressure or a direct sys_exec caller appears.)

findings.title: do_kill() unlinks a binsem waiter without restoring node->sem, breaking the invariant binsem_op() relies on
findings.detail:
do_kill() (line 338) on a victim whose status is TASK_BLOCKED takes the else-branch and calls reclaim_pcb() (line 295), which does `list_del(&task->list)`. If the victim was blocked inside binsem_op(BINSEM_OP_LOCK) it is sitting in binsem_nodes[id].block_queue and that semaphore's `sem` is already negative. release_resources()/release_binsem() only give back the semaphores the victim *holds* (task->binsem_id[]); nothing compensates the pending wait, so the victim is spliced out of block_queue while `sem` stays negative. kernel/locking/binsem.c (given, unmodifiable) assumes `sem <= 0 => block_queue non-empty`: its UNLOCK path does `node->sem++; if (node->sem <= 0) { unblocked_pcb = list_entry(node->block_queue.next, pcb_t, list); unblocked_pcb->binsem_id[unblocked_pcb->binsem_num++] = binsem_id; do_unblock(...); }` with no emptiness check.

Concrete failure: run `exec consensus` (9 tasks contend on barrier->binsem_id via mthread_barrier_wait), then `kill <pid>` for a task that is queued on the binsem (sem == -1, one waiter). reclaim_pcb removes it, leaving sem == -1 and an empty queue. The holder's next UNLOCK does sem++ -> 0, sees `sem <= 0`, and computes list_entry(&node->block_queue, pcb_t, list) == (char*)&node->block_queue - 40, i.e. a fabricated pcb_t inside the binsem_nodes[] array. It then writes binsem_id[binsem_num] through that pointer (arbitrary 4-byte store, binsem_num read from garbage at &block_queue+432) and calls do_unblock() on the list head itself, which NULLs the head's next/prev and links the binsem head node into ready_queue. On the next scheduler() pass max_priority_node() reads mask/ready_tick/priority out of binsem_nodes[] and scheduler() then executes `set_satp(SATP_MODE_SV39, 0, next->pgdir >> 12)` with a garbage pgdir -> immediate unrecoverable fault. Also every later list_empty() on that binsem sees next == NULL != head, so it never recovers.

findings.title: do_kill() releases the victim's resources while the victim is still running on the other hart
findings.detail:
do_kill() calls `release_resources(victim)` (line 362) *before* the TASK_RUNNING check (line 364) that defers teardown to the other hart. For a victim executing on the other hart, its held binary semaphores are handed to other tasks (release_binsem, line 260) and task->binsem_num is zeroed while the victim is still inside its critical section and keeps running user code for up to a full timer_interval.

Concrete failure: two consensus tasks A (hart 0) and B (hart 1). B holds barrier->binsem_id and is between `barrier->reached++` and `sys_binsem_op(UNLOCK)`. The shell on hart 0 runs `kill <B>`. release_binsem() does sem++ and hands the lock to waiter C, which now enters the barrier critical section concurrently with B -> lost update on barrier->reached, barrier never completes. Worse, B then executes its own sys_binsem_op(UNLOCK): binsem_op does `node->sem++` a second time (double release, sem now above 1, mutual exclusion permanently broken) and `current_running[cpu_id]->binsem_num--` taking B's binsem_num to -1. B's next BINSEM_OP_LOCK writes `binsem_id[-1]`, i.e. the 4 bytes immediately before the binsem_id array, which is the upper half of pcb_t.wait_list.prev (binsem_id is at offset 72, wait_list at 56..71) -> B's wait_list head is corrupted and any later list op on it faults. The kill also does not stop B from running until its next trap.

findings.title: TASK_KILLED is silently lost if the victim blocks before its next reschedule, so kill() is a no-op after resources were already released
findings.detail:
do_kill() defers teardown by setting `victim->status = TASK_KILLED` (line 367) and relies on scheduler()'s `else if (prev->status == TASK_KILLED)` branch (line 66) firing on the victim's hart. But status is a single field that do_block() (line 593) overwrites unconditionally with TASK_BLOCKED. If the flagged victim reaches any blocking call before its next timer tick -- do_sleep(), binsem_op(LOCK), futex_wait(), do_waitpid() -- the TASK_KILLED marker is destroyed. scheduler() then sees prev->status == TASK_BLOCKED, takes neither branch, and the process is left intact in the sleep/block queue with its address space and pcb slot alive; do_unblock() later marks it TASK_READY and it runs forever.

Concrete failure: `exec consensus` then `kill <pid>` of a task currently running on the other hart. consensus.c calls sys_sleep(2) every loop iteration (lines 90, 98, 120), so within the ~10 ms window before the victim's next timer interrupt it almost always enters do_sleep -> do_block. The shell prints "Task(pid=N) killed" but the task keeps running; meanwhile release_resources() already gave away its semaphores, drained its wait_list and cleared its timer node, so it resumes in the inconsistent state described in the previous finding.

findings.title: Waiters woken by do_kill() re-block on a wait_list that reclaim_pcb() never drains again -> do_waitpid() hangs forever
findings.detail:
release_resources() (line 278) drains child->wait_list at kill time, but for a victim running on the other hart do_kill() only sets TASK_KILLED; the victim does not become TASK_ZOMBIE/TASK_EXITED until that hart next enters scheduler(). reclaim_pcb() (line 295) does not touch wait_list, so there is no second wakeup.

Concrete failure: parent P is blocked in do_waitpid(C) on C->wait_list; C runs on hart 1. Hart 0 executes do_kill(C): release_resources wakes P (do_unblock -> ready_queue), then C->status = TASK_KILLED. Hart 0's next scheduler() picks P, P retries the rewound `ecall` (do_waitpid, line 405) and finds C->status == TASK_KILLED, which is neither TASK_ZOMBIE nor TASK_EXITED, so it falls through to `do_block(&P->list, &C->wait_list)` at line 417. Up to a full timer interval later hart 1's scheduler() runs reclaim_pcb(C), which sets ZOMBIE/EXITED but never drains C->wait_list -> P blocks permanently. In AUTO_CLEANUP mode it gets worse: main.c's idle loop then sets C->pid = -1, do_exec reuses the slot and calls `init_list_head(&new_pcb->wait_list)` (line 226), leaving P's list node pointing at a re-initialised head -- a dangling node that will splice garbage into whatever queue touches it next.

findings.title: scheduler() publishes the dying task's pcb and kernel stack to main.c's lock-free idle loop while that stack is still in use
findings.detail:
For AUTO_CLEANUP_ON_EXIT (the mode test_shell.c and consensus.c always use), reclaim_pcb() at line 304 does `list_add_tail(&task->list, &kernel_pcb[0].wait_list)` from inside scheduler(), i.e. before do_exit() has unwound. main.c's idle loop is the consumer and it runs *outside* the global kernel lock -- lock_kernel/unlock_kernel are only called from exception_handler_entry and ret_from_exception (arch/riscv/kernel/entry.S:199,157); main()'s `while(1)` after sbi_set_timer holds nothing but its own CSR_SIE mask, which has no effect on the other hart.

After scheduler() returns, the exiting task on hart 1 still writes to that kernel stack: do_exit()'s epilogue, then handle_syscall()'s `regs->regs[10] = syscall[...](...)` (kernel/syscall/syscall.c:9) storing into the trap frame, then `call unlock_kernel` in ret_from_exception which pushes onto the same sp (RESTORE_CONTEXT has not switched sp yet). Concretely: hart 1 runs `exit` -> reclaim_pcb enqueues the pcb; hart 0, sitting in main()'s cleanup loop, calls free_user_page(kva2pa(kernel_stack_base - PAGE_SIZE)) marking user_page[i].valid = 0 and sets clean_pcb->pid = -1; the very next alloc_user_page() (a page fault or do_exec on either hart) hands out that frame and memsets it to zero -> hart 1's trap frame and saved return addresses are wiped mid-unwind. The pid = -1 also lets do_exec() reuse the slot and rewrite preempt_count/kernel_sp/pgdir while hart 1's tp still points at that pcb and is about to run enable_preempt() on it. do_waitpid()'s reap path (line 407) frees the same frame independently, so a concurrent reap and idle-loop pass double-free it, and the list_del at line 408 can NULL the node the idle loop is iterating (`clean_node = clean_node->next; list_del(clean_node->prev);`).

findings.title: do_kill()/do_waitpid() match free pcb slots when pid == -1, then walk an uninitialised wait_list
findings.detail:
Both lookups (lines 343-348 and 392-397) accept `pcb[i].pid == pid` without excluding the free-slot sentinel -1. A never-used slot lives in BSS, so status == 0 == TASK_BLOCKED and wait_list == {NULL, NULL} (only init_pcb() and do_exec() run init_list_head on it).

Concrete failure: any user program calling sys_kill(-1) (or `kill /` in the shell, since tiny_libc atoi maps '/' to -1) selects the first free slot, passes the TASK_EXITED/ZOMBIE/KILLED guard, and enters release_resources(). `list_empty(&task->wait_list)` evaluates NULL == &wait_list -> false, so it calls do_unblock(NULL) -> list_del(NULL) dereferences address 8 in S-mode. handle_page_fault (kernel/mm/mm.c:395) sees stval < the user limit and maps a _PAGE_USER page at VA 0 in the current pgdir; with SUM clear the retried kernel load faults again, giving an unbreakable page-fault loop that wedges the hart with the global kernel lock held. sys_waitpid(-1) reaches the same uninitialised head through do_block()/list_add_tail (`head->prev` is NULL -> NULL->next store).

result.reason: Could not refute; the claim is confirmed by the sources. In /workspace/Project4-Virtual_Memory_Management/kernel/sched/sched.c:135-177, init_user_stack() maps exactly one frame (alloc_page_helper at line 138, which per mm.c:213-239 returns the kva of a single frame) and then copies argv strings downward with `sp -= strlen(argv[i]) + 1` (lines 155-160) and the argv array (lines 163-169) with no check that sp stays >= top_va - PAGE_SIZE. Only argc is clamped (<= MAX_EXEC_ARGC = 16); per-string and total byte length are unbounded and fully user-controlled: handle_syscall (kernel/syscall/syscall.c:9-13) passes a0-a3 straight to do_exec (init/main.c:131), and do_exec (sched.c:185-249) calls enable_sum() and forwards argc/argv with no copy-in or length validation; kernel strlen (libs/string.c:21) is an unbounded scan. STACK_KVA(sp) below the frame base therefore writes into the physically preceding frame through the direct map (pa2kva = pa + 0xffffffc000000000, pgtable.h:139), and it cannot fault: boot.c:35-44 maps pa 0x50000000-0x60000000 with R/W/X/A/D via 128 2MB leaves, so the corruption is silent. Arithmetic checks out: usable string space is 4096 - 8*(argc+1) = 3960 at argc=16, so 16 x ~300-byte args puts sp ~840 bytes below the frame base; a hostile program passing 16 pointers to 4KB buffers overruns ~15 frames. Refinement to the claim: because init_page_table (mm.c:247-266) allocates the 5 code frames before the stack frame and alloc_user_page is first-fit (mm.c:50-77), on an unfragmented free list the frames just below the stack frame are the new process's own freshly loaded ELF text (PT_LOAD 0xf000, memsz ~0x3e98), so the immediate observable failure is self-corruption of the just-loaded image; cross-process corruption occurs once the free list is fragmented by exited processes. The 0x50fff000/kernel-heap variant is unlikely since frame 0 (pa 0x51000000) is permanently held by the shell's 0xf000 code page, but that was stated conditionally. The shell path is also real (test_shell.c:246-275 passes argc-1 up to 11 while _argv has only 9 entries, so the kernel strlen()s out-of-bounds pointers; handle_page_fault at mm.c:395-407 even maps bogus user addresses on demand instead of trapping), though its string volume is capped by the ~54-char input line, making the direct sys_exec path the decisive trigger.

The code observation is literally true (init_user_stack clamps a local argc at sched.c:147-152 while do_exec passes the raw argc at sched.c:248-249), but no concrete failure follows. Divergence requires argc > MAX_EXEC_ARGC(16), argc < 0, or argv == NULL with argc > 0, and no caller in the unmodifiable tree can produce any of those: init/main.c:63-121 sets up the shell with its own 4-arg static init_pcb_stack and never uses argc/init_user_stack; test/consensus.c:86 passes argc=2 with a valid 2-entry array; test/test_shell.c:271-275 passes argc-1 with a 9-slot _argv. Scenario A (sys_exec("rw", 20, argv20, ...) with 20 valid entries) requires a user program that does not and cannot exist here; moreover the shell path proves the proposed fix is inert: the shell's parser (test_shell.c:124-148) only warns and keeps counting, while _argv holds just 9 valid pointers, so for argc-1 in 10..16 the kernel already strlen()s out-of-bounds garbage pointers from the shell's stack in a range where the clamp is a no-op and a0 matches the array exactly - propagating the clamped argc would prevent nothing. Scenario A's endpoint is also pre-existing by design: test/rw.c:16 writes *(long*)mem1 for a user-typed address, so `exec rw 0x8000000000` already reaches handle_other via mm.c:399-402. Scenario B is mechanically wrong: with argv_va=0xf0000fff8 and a0=2 the child reads argv[1] at 0xf00010000, which is far below the 1<<38 kernel-fault threshold, so handle_page_fault (mm.c:395-407) demand-maps it through alloc_page_helper; the resulting 0 passed to atol (tiny_libc/atol.c) is likewise demand-mapped at va 0. No panic, no corruption - and no in-tree caller passes NULL argv with nonzero argc. This is a latent inconsistency in optional hardening, not a demonstrable defect.

findings.title: write_to_sd copies the victim frame to disk before invalidating its PTE, so concurrent user writes on the other hart are silently lost
findings.detail: write_to_sd() (mm.c:123-149) does `sbi_sd_write(pa, ...)` first (line 134) and only afterwards clears _PAGE_PRESENT / sets _PAGE_SOFT / calls flush_tlb_all() (lines 140-147). The kernel lock (kernel/sched/smp.c:30) is released by ret_from_exception before `sret` (arch/riscv/kernel/entry.S:157), so while hart 0 is inside write_to_sd, hart 1 can be executing user code in the very address space that owns the victim frame. Concrete failure: process P runs on hart 1 with va V -> frame F mapped writable (alloc_page_helper always grants _PAGE_WRITE|_PAGE_DIRTY, mm.c:233). Hart 0 takes a page fault for another task, alloc_user_page (mm.c:60-65) finds no free frame, selete_page() returns F, write_to_sd snapshots F to swap slot i. Hart 1 then stores 0xdead to V — the PTE is still present and its TLB entry is still valid, so the store lands in F. Hart 0 now clears _PAGE_PRESENT, flushes, frees F, memsets it (mm.c:75) and hands it to the new owner. When P later faults on V, alloc_page_helper reads back the pre-store copy from slot i: P's write has vanished with no error. The invalidate+shootdown must happen before the sbi_sd_write, not after. The same window also lets a stale remote TLB entry write into a frame hart 0 has already memset and reassigned to a different process.

findings.title: Eviction can steal the caller's own user pages mid-syscall; the resulting S-mode page fault deadlocks on the non-recursive kernel lock
findings.detail: do_exec() (sched.c:185-256) calls enable_sum() at line 189 and keeps user pointers `file_name` and `argv[]` (which point into the *caller's* address space) live across init_page_table() (line 219, ~6 frames), alloc_user_page() for the kernel stack (line 221) and load_elf() (line 244, more frames). Every one of those may run alloc_user_page -> selete_page(), and selete_page (mm.c:104-116) skips only `pin` and `pgtable == NULL` frames — the shell's own stack page holding argv[i] and the argv strings is an ordinary unpinned frame and is a legal victim. init_user_stack() then dereferences it at sched.c:156-158 (`strlen(argv[i])`, `memcpy(..., argv[i], len)`). Because the page is now _PAGE_SOFT, that load traps in S-mode; exception_handler_entry unconditionally executes `call lock_kernel` (arch/riscv/kernel/entry.S:199) and lock_kernel is a plain non-recursive spin_lock_acquire (kernel/sched/smp.c:30, kernel/locking/lock.c:9-17) that this hart already holds — both harts wedge forever, with no console output. Nothing pins the caller's argv/file_name pages (or copies them into kernel memory) for the duration of the call, and handle_page_fault has no way to report failure. The same hazard applies to do_process_show/do_show_exec, which write into a user buffer under SUM.

findings.title: selete_page clears _PAGE_ACCESSED without a TLB shootdown, so the reference bit is never re-set and NRU degenerates
findings.detail: selete_page (mm.c:111-114) does `clear_attribute(user_page[i].pgtable, _PAGE_ACCESSED)` and continues, with no local_flush_tlb_page/flush_tlb_all anywhere in the sweep (the only flush is inside write_to_sd, mm.c:147, after a victim is already chosen). On RISC-V the A bit is written by the page-table walker; a hit in the TLB performs no walk, so once the in-memory bit has been cleared it stays clear for every page whose translation is still cached. Concrete failure: under memory pressure the first clock sweep clears A on all resident frames; on the second sweep every frame looks unreferenced, so the very first candidate is evicted regardless of how hot it is — including the page holding the instruction that just faulted or the current user stack page, which immediately refaults and forces another eviction. The intended second-chance behaviour never happens and the policy degrades to plain FIFO with extra 4 KB disk writes.

findings.title: alloc_user_page zeroes the whole 4 KB frame that the swap-in path immediately overwrites with sbi_sd_read
findings.detail: alloc_user_page unconditionally does `memset((void*)pa2kva(pa), 0, PAGE_SIZE)` (mm.c:75) before returning. In the swap-in branch of alloc_page_helper (mm.c:222-223) the very next statement is `sbi_sd_read((unsigned int)pa, PAGE_SD_BLOCKS, ...)`, which overwrites all 4096 bytes. Every page brought back from swap therefore pays a full-page zeroing that is discarded — and the zeroing happens on the critical path of a page fault, with the global kernel lock held and both harts serialised behind it. The memset is only needed on the fresh-allocation path (mm.c:229) where it prevents leaking the previous owner's data; the swap-in path should skip it (e.g. by an extra argument or by allocating raw and zeroing at the call site).

findings.title: Swap area holds only 256 slots for 53248 frames and exhausting it panics the kernel instead of failing the allocation
findings.detail: write_to_sd allocates a slot with a linear scan and `assert(i != DISK_PAGE_NUM)` (mm.c:126-131); DISK_PAGE_NUM is 256 while USER_PAGE_NUM is (0x5e000000-0x51000000)/4096 = 53248. Every eviction consumes a slot unconditionally — there is no _PAGE_DIRTY check, so clean, never-written pages (the read-only ELF text pages that init_page_table maps at mm.c:259-261, which could simply be dropped and reloaded) burn slots too. Once physical memory fills, the 257th eviction hits assert(0) and takes down the whole kernel rather than failing the one allocation; alloc_user_page (mm.c:50) has no failure return and handle_page_fault (mm.c:406) ignores the result, so there is no path to kill just the offending process. do_exec's guard `free_page_num() < EXEC_MIN_FREE_PAGES` (sched.c:212) counts physical frames only and never looks at disk_page[], so it cannot prevent this. selete_page's own `assert(0)` (mm.c:119) is the same class of unrecoverable exit.

result.reason: Could not refute; the defect is real and confirmed against the sources. do_kill() (/workspace/Project4-Virtual_Memory_Management/kernel/sched/sched.c:362-367) calls release_resources(victim) and then, for a victim that is TASK_RUNNING on the other hart, only records the kill by writing victim->status = TASK_KILLED. That marker is consumed nowhere except scheduler()'s `else if (prev->status == TASK_KILLED)` at sched.c:66 (grep for TASK_KILLED over the whole tree returns only sched.h:61 and sched.c:{66,320,350,364,367}), and pcb_t (include/os/sched.h:75-126) has no separate kill flag, so status is the sole channel. do_block() at sched.c:593-598 overwrites status unconditionally with TASK_BLOCKED, so any blocking call the victim makes before its next scheduler() invocation destroys the flag: do_sleep (sched.c:332), do_waitpid (sched.c:417 — itself new code), kernel/locking/binsem.c:39, kernel/locking/futex.c:55, kernel/syscall/mailbox.c:63,85. scheduler() then takes neither branch, the task stays queued with its pgdir alive and its pcb slot occupied, and do_unblock (sched.c:601) later marks it TASK_READY so it keeps running after release_binsem() already handed its semaphores to an heir and its wait_list was drained. Nothing rescues this: the global kernel lock (entry.S: lock_kernel in exception_handler_entry, unlock_kernel in ret_from_exception) only guarantees the victim is in user mode or spinning while do_kill runs, and there is no reschedule IPI to the peer hart (sbi_send_ipi appears only at kernel/sched/smp.c:27, boot-time hart wakeup). The victim hart's own next scheduler() comes either from reset_irq_timer() (kernel/irq/irq.c, timer_interval = time_base/100 ~= 10 ms) or from a blocking path that has already clobbered the flag. The concrete scenario is reachable: test/test_shell.c:345 calls sys_kill and prints "Task(pid=N) killed" on return 1; do_exec inherits the shell's mask (sched.c:236, init/main.c pcb[0].mask = 3) so children run on hart 1; test/consensus.c:90,98,120 call sys_sleep(2) and each loop iteration also runs mthread_barrier_wait -> sys_binsem_op(LOCK)/sys_futex_wait (tiny_libc/mthread.c:13-25), both reaching do_block. Only caveat, which does not change correctness: catching the victim in TASK_RUNNING is roughly 1/N likely for N consensus tasks (they are mostly TASK_BLOCKED, where do_kill's else branch tears down correctly), but conditional on that the victim is in the short non-blocking stretch of its loop and will reach do_block well within the ~10 ms before its next tick, so the marker is almost certainly lost.

Could not refute; every premise verified. (1) init/main.c:94-96 sets pcb[i].pid = -1 for ALL NUM_MAX_TASK slots and only calls init_list_head(&pcb[0].wait_list) at line 105, so slots 1..N-1 keep wait_list == {NULL, NULL} from BSS; init_list_head at sched.c:226 only runs when do_exec allocates a slot. (2) TASK_BLOCKED is the first enumerator in include/os/sched.h:56, so a pristine slot's status == 0 == TASK_BLOCKED and passes do_kill's EXITED/ZOMBIE/KILLED guard. (3) git diff confirms both lookups are NEW code: `if (pcb[i].pid == pid)` at kernel/sched/sched.c:337 (do_kill) and :392 (do_waitpid), with no `pid != -1` filter — while the same new code writes the sentinel (do_waitpid `child->pid = -1;` at :410) and reads it in alloc_pcb (:199-202, comment "`pid == -1` marks an unused slot"). (4) release_resources (sched.c:275-277) is `while (!list_empty(&task->wait_list)) do_unblock(task->wait_list.next);`; list_empty is head->next == head (list.h:106), so NULL != &wait_list -> loop entered with do_unblock(NULL), and since do_unblock never modifies task->wait_list the loop is also non-terminating — a hang with preempt disabled and the global kernel lock held. (5) struct list_node is {next, prev} (list.h:42-45), so list_del(NULL) reads offset 8 -> load from VA 8, exactly as claimed; list_add_tail then stores through NULL at VA 0. (6) handle_page_fault (kernel/mm/mm.c:395-406) only escalates when stval >= (1lu << (VPN2_SHIFT+PPN_BITS-1)); stval==8 is below that, so it calls alloc_page_helper(8, current pgdir) and retries. (7) Reachable from the stock shell: tiny_libc/string.c:80-88 atoi has no sign/digit validation so atoi("/") == '/' - '0' == -1; test/test_shell.c:335-345 only blocks pid 0 and 1 before sys_kill(pid); tiny_libc/syscall.c:19-22 passes (long)pid; kernel/syscall/syscall.c:9 forwards regs[10] untouched; init/main.c:134-135 wires do_kill/do_waitpid with no wrapper. Only cosmetic errors in the report: line numbers are 336-342 / 391-397 rather than 343-348 / 392-397, and the dominant symptom is the non-terminating while loop in release_resources rather than a single NULL deref.

Claim holds; I could not refute it. In /workspace/Project4-Virtual_Memory_Management/kernel/sched/sched.c, release_resources() (line 278, drain loop at 306-307) is the ONLY code in the entire tree that drains a pcb's wait_list — verified with `grep -rn wait_list`: the only other references are init_list_head in do_exec (line 228), do_block in do_waitpid (line 441), and kernel_pcb[0].wait_list, which is the unrelated AUTO-cleanup queue drained by init/main.c:204-215. do_kill() calls release_resources(victim) at line 362 and then, for a victim TASK_RUNNING on the other hart, only sets victim->status = TASK_KILLED (line 367). Neither scheduler()'s dying-task path (lines 98-102) nor reclaim_pcb() (295-306) ever touches wait_list, so there is no second wakeup. do_waitpid() line 405 tests only TASK_ZOMBIE/TASK_EXITED; TASK_KILLED is a distinct enum value (include/os/sched.h:56-62), so a parent that retries the rewound ecall inside the KILLED-but-not-yet-reclaimed window falls through to do_block(&cur->list, &child->wait_list) at line 441 and is never woken again. The window is genuinely open, not theoretical: arch/riscv/kernel/entry.S takes the global kernel lock only at trap entry (line 199) and releases it in ret_from_exception (line 157), so hart 1 keeps running the victim in user mode after hart 0 returns from do_kill and only reaches scheduler() at its own independent timer tick (kernel/irq/irq.c:105-112), up to one timer_interval later; hart 0's tick can pick the just-unblocked parent out of ready_queue before that. list_del (include/os/list.h:80-87) NULLs the node and is idempotent, so the double delete on the dying pcb is harmless — that does not rescue the waiter. The AUTO_CLEANUP escalation is also real: init/main.c:209 sets pid = -1 and do_exec line 228 re-inits wait_list, leaving the parent's node pointing at a re-initialised head; a later list_del on that stale node (e.g. reclaim_pcb if the parent is itself killed) writes through the head and silently unlinks a legitimate new waiter. Only mitigating fact found: no shipped user program actually calls sys_waitpid (it is linked into every ELF from tiny_libc/syscall.c but test/*.c only use sys_exec/sys_kill), so the default test run may not trip it — but SYSCALL_WAITPID is registered in init/main.c:135 and is required lab functionality, so this is a genuine latent permanent hang in the new code.

findings.title: shm_page_dt() accepts kernel-half addresses; find_pte() walks the kernel's 2MB leaf entries as if they were page tables
findings.detail: shm_page_dt() (line 368) passes the raw user-supplied `addr` straight to find_pte() with no range check, and find_pte() (line 189) tests only `_PAGE_PRESENT` on the level-2/level-1 entries — it never checks for R/W/X, i.e. for a superpage leaf. Every user pgdir contains the kernel window (`pgdir_kva[0x101]` copied by init_page_table), whose level-1 entries 0x80..0xff are 2MB *leaf* mappings of physical 0x50000000-0x60000000. So for a kernel VA the walk descends one level too far and returns `pa2kva(2MB-region base) + vpn0*8` — a pointer at an arbitrary 8-byte word of real memory, which shm_page_dt then interprets as a PTE. Reproduced by running the real mm.c on the host: process 1 attaches key 77 (frame 0x5100c000, count=1); process 0 plants the qword 0x14403001 (PRESENT + pfn of 0x5100c000) at the start of a 2MB-aligned frame it owns (0x51200000) and calls sys_shmpage_dt(0xffffffc051200000). Result: that kernel word is zeroed, shm_page[77].count drops 1->0, and free_user_page() releases the shared frame while process 1's PTE at 0x1000 still points at it — the frame is then handed out to the next alloc_user_page() caller underneath a live mapping. Two lines fix it: reject `addr` outside [SHM_VA_BEGIN, SHM_VA_END) in shm_page_dt(), and make find_pte()/walk_pgdir() bail out when an intermediate entry has any of _PAGE_READ|_PAGE_WRITE|_PAGE_EXEC set.

findings.title: handle_page_fault() silently ignores faults it cannot resolve, so the hart retries the instruction forever
findings.detail: handle_page_fault() (line 395) forwards every user-half stval to alloc_page_helper(), which returns without touching anything when the leaf PTE already has _PAGE_PRESENT (line 216). `cause` is ignored and `regs->sepc` is untouched, so ret_from_exception re-executes the faulting instruction, which faults identically — an endless fault loop with no diagnostic. This is reachable on the normal panic path: entry.S clears SR_SUM on trap entry (`li t0, SR_SUM | SR_FS; csrc sstatus, t0`), and handle_other() then walks the user frame pointer (`while (fp > 0x10000) { prev_ra = *(uintptr_t*)(fp-8); ... }` in kernel/irq/irq.c) with SUM clear. An S-mode access to a U=1 page with SUM=0 raises a load *page* fault whose stval is a mapped user stack address, so handle_page_fault does nothing and the machine wedges after printing the register dump — including for the kernel-address faults this very function routes to handle_other. Same shape for an instruction fetch out of a shared page, which shm_page_get() maps without _PAGE_EXEC (line 353). The handler should treat 'PTE already present' (or a permission mismatch against `cause`) as fatal and call handle_other().

findings.title: Shared-memory keys are folded with `key % SHM_PAGE_NUM` and no key is stored, so distinct keys silently share one page
findings.detail: shm_page_get() (line 337) selects the descriptor with `&shm_page[(uint32_t)key % SHM_PAGE_NUM]` (SHM_PAGE_NUM = 100) and nothing anywhere records which key owns a slot; shm_page_t only holds {count, pa}. Two unrelated programs using keys that are congruent mod 100 — e.g. 42 (consensus's SHMP_KEY) and 142, or 7 and 107 — are handed the same physical frame and the same refcount, so each one sees the other's writes and either can trigger the count==0 free while the other is still attached. mm.c already owns the descriptor table, so a parallel `static int shm_key[SHM_PAGE_NUM];` plus a linear search for a matching-or-free slot (and clearing it when count hits 0 in shm_page_dt/free_process_user_page) removes the aliasing.

result.reason: The claim's central premise — that no TLB shootdown follows the A-bit clears — is factually wrong. selete_page() has exactly one caller, alloc_user_page() at /workspace/Project4-Virtual_Memory_Management/kernel/mm/mm.c:62-63, which does `pa = selete_page(); write_to_sd(pa);` unconditionally and back-to-back. write_to_sd() ends with flush_tlb_all() (mm.c:147), which executes after every clear_attribute(..., _PAGE_ACCESSED) in the sweep (those all happen inside selete_page, which has already returned) and before control returns to user code. The reviewer conflates "after a victim is already chosen" with "too late to matter": the flush is not scoped to the victim. flush_tlb_all() (pgtable.h:28-32) is local_flush_tlb_all() — a bare `sfence.vma` with no rs1/rs2, invalidating ALL address-translation cache entries for all VAs and ASIDs — plus sbi_remote_sfence_vma(NULL, 0, -1), which covers the other hart. So every frame whose A bit was cleared in the sweep also loses its cached translation; its next access takes a TLB miss, the walker runs, and hardware re-sets A. This is the standard batched-shootdown idiom (same as Linux's clock sweep); per-page flushes in the loop would cost more for identical semantics. A second, independent flush makes the scenario impossible regardless: scheduler() at kernel/sched/sched.c:116-117 calls set_satp() (which itself begins with `sfence.vma`, pgtable.h:56) followed by local_flush_tlb_all(), so the local TLB is emptied at every context switch. alloc_page_helper() also flushes after installing the new PTE (mm.c:235). Consequently the described failure does not occur: after sweep N + global flush, the hot pages (the faulting instruction's page, which re-executes immediately after handle_page_fault returns, and the current user stack page) are re-walked and get A re-set, so at sweep N+1 they are marked accessed and correctly receive their second chance. The policy does not degenerate to FIFO. The only defensible criticism is a performance one (flush_tlb_all plus an IPI per eviction is heavier than targeted local_flush_tlb_page calls), which is a simplicity tradeoff, not the correctness defect claimed.

REFUTED. The trap/lock mechanics the reviewer describes are accurate in the abstract (entry.S `bnez tp` -> from_user -> `call lock_kernel`, and kernel/locking/lock.c's spin_lock_try_acquire is non-recursive, so an S-mode fault taken while holding the kernel lock would spin forever), but neither concrete trigger is reachable, and the residual exposure belongs to the given framework, not the new code.

(1) Trigger 2 (do_exec evicting the caller's own argv page) is impossible by construction of the new code. /workspace/Project4-Virtual_Memory_Management/kernel/sched/sched.c:247 gates the whole path on `free_page_num() < EXEC_MIN_FREE_PAGES` (16, defined line 43) and returns -2 *before* `init_page_table()` at line 254. The exec path then allocates at most 7 user frames: init_page_table (/workspace/Project4-Virtual_Memory_Management/kernel/mm/mm.c) maps USER_CODE_BEGIN 0xf000 .. USER_CODE_END 0x14000 = 5 pages plus the 0xf0000f000 stack page (6), and sched.c:256 takes 1 pinned frame for the kernel stack (7). load_elf's single PT_LOAD (vaddr 0xf000, memsz 0x3e98) walks 0xf000/0x10000/0x11000/0x12000, all already mapped, so alloc_page_helper returns the existing frame and allocates nothing; init_user_stack's alloc_page_helper hits the same already-mapped 0xf0000f000 page. alloc_user_page only enters the selete_page()/write_to_sd() branch when the scan finds zero free frames (`i == USER_PAGE_NUM`); with >=16 free on entry and <=7 consumed, at least 9 always remain, so selete_page() is never reached from do_exec. The count cannot be drained concurrently either: do_exec runs with disable_preempt() and under the global kernel lock (taken in exception_handler_entry, dropped in ret_from_exception), every user-frame allocation in the tree is reached through a trap, and the only lock-free kernel loop (init/main.c idle) merely calls free_user_page, which raises the free count.

(2) Trigger 1 (a never-touched pointer such as 0x20000000) has no caller. The only sys_exec caller in the tree is /workspace/Project4-Virtual_Memory_Management/test/test_shell.c:275, which passes `argv[1]` and `_argv[]` - stack locals written by the shell's own parser and the copy loop at lines 271-274 in user mode immediately before the ecall, hence resident. Exec'd children get their full ELF memsz mapped by load_elf/alloc_page_helper, and arch/riscv/crt0.S clears .bss, so no statically allocated user object is ever non-resident. Reproducing the fault requires writing a new user program that deliberately hands the kernel an address it never touched.

(3) Even then it is not a new-code defect: dereferencing user pointers under SUM without validation is the framework's own convention, present in given, unmodifiable code (drivers/screen.c screen_write, the tools-generated get_elf_file strcmp that init/main.c:118 also calls, mailbox/futex), and the fatality comes entirely from given files (entry.S's from_user branch plus the non-recursive kernel_lock in kernel/sched/smp.c and kernel/locking/lock.c). The new handle_page_fault in mm.c services user-mode faults correctly; it simply can never be entered for a kernel-mode fault, and no new code assumes otherwise.

(4) Ancillary: the swap subsystem is capped at DISK_PAGE_NUM=256 slots against 53248 user frames (208 MB), and write_to_sd asserts when the slots run out, so a sustained memory-pressure workload panics on that assert long before it could evict argv pages in a loop.

Note: the cited line numbers (156-158, 189, 219-246) match the identical copy at /workspace/Project5-Device_Driver/kernel/sched/sched.c rather than the P4 file; that copy carries the same guard (EXEC_MIN_FREE_PAGES at line 43, checked at 212 before init_page_table at 219), so the refutation holds there too.

Refuted. The claim is accurate that reclaim_pcb() (sched.c:367) publishes from inside scheduler() and that main()'s idle loop (init/main.c:212-227) consumes without the kernel lock (lock_kernel/unlock_kernel exist only at entry.S:199 and :157). But the claimed failure chain is blocked:

1) The idle loop's writes are inert w.r.t. the stack contents. free_user_page() (mm.c:80-83) is only `user_page[i].valid = 0`; it does not touch the frame. Contents change only in alloc_user_page()'s memset (mm.c:75).

2) Every reallocation path needs the kernel lock, which hart 1 holds through the entire unwind. The complete set of allocation sites outside boot is do_exec (sched.c:160,260,262,286), shm_page_get (mm.c:342) and handle_page_fault (mm.c:406) — all reached only via exception_handler_entry's `call lock_kernel`. main.c:99,114 run before wakeup_other_hart() and before setup_exception(). Hart 1 holds the lock from entry.S:199 until entry.S:157, covering do_exit's epilogue, handle_syscall's `regs->regs[10] = ...`, and the return through interrupt_helper. So "the very next alloc_user_page() hands out that frame and memsets it -> trap frame wiped mid-unwind" cannot happen.

3) The trap-frame store is a dead store regardless: RESTORE_CONTEXT starts with `ld sp, PCB_KERNEL_SP(tp)` (entry.S:56) using tp reloaded from current_cpu_running at entry.S:156 — the incoming task. The dying task's regs_context_t is never read back.

4) The pcb-reuse sub-claim fails the same way: do_exit's enable_preempt() writes the dying pcb's preempt_count while hart 1 still holds the lock, so a concurrent do_exec is impossible; and entry.S reloads tp to the new task BEFORE `call unlock_kernel`, so the dying pcb is never referenced after the release. Also sstatus.SIE is hardware-cleared on trap entry and enable_preempt only touches the sie mask CSR, so no nested trap re-enters on the dying stack.

5) The do_waitpid double-free path is unreachable: `grep -rn waitpid test/ tiny_libc/` shows sys_waitpid is never called by any test (test_shell.c:275 and consensus.c:86 use AUTO_CLEANUP_ON_EXIT and never wait), and for ENTER_ZOMBIE_ON_EXIT reclaim_pcb deliberately does not enqueue onto kernel_pcb[0].wait_list (sched.c:361-368), so the reap path and the idle loop are mutually exclusive by construction.

Residual, not reportable: I compiled smp.c at the project's -O0 and confirmed unlock_kernel is not a tail call — it emits `ld ra,8(sp); ld s0,0(sp)` after spin_lock_release returns, i.e. two reads of the dying stack after the release store. Exploiting that requires another hart to win the lock and run the whole trap dispatch into alloc_user_page's scan + memset, hitting that exact frame, within hart 1's next ~4 instructions. Not a demonstrable failure, and it is a property of the unmodifiable entry.S/smp.c that occurs on every trap return. Likewise the unlocked list_del vs. locked list_add_tail on kernel_pcb[0].wait_list is forced by the given init/main.c, which hard-codes that list, that free_user_page call, and lock-free iteration; no conforming implementation can take a lock the consumer does not take.

Minor: the claim's line numbers (304, 407, 408) do not match this file — those lines are release_binsem and do_kill; the cited constructs are at 367, 470, 471.

The factual premise is accurate but it is not a defect, and both proposed remedies are worse than the code as written.

1) No incorrect behavior is alleged or possible. The claim itself concedes the code is correct (the memset "prevents leaking the previous owner's data") and only alleges redundant work. There is no input, state, or interleaving that produces a wrong result, a crash, or a hang. Confirmed: PAGE_SD_BLOCKS = PAGE_SIZE / SD_BLOCK_SIZE = 8 (include/os/mm.h:120-121), so sbi_sd_read at /workspace/Project4-Virtual_Memory_Management/kernel/mm/mm.c:223 does cover all 4096 bytes — the memset is functionally dead on that one path, and dead-but-harmless.

2) The suggested fix "by an extra argument" is impossible without breaking given, unmodifiable code. `extern ptr_t alloc_user_page(uint8_t pin, PTE* pgtable);` is pre-existing, not new: `git show HEAD:Project4-Virtual_Memory_Management/include/os/mm.h` shows that exact declaration (the mm.h diff only appends alloc_page_helper/find_pte and the SHM/SD macros at the end). And /workspace/Project4-Virtual_Memory_Management/init/main.c:99 — a given file — calls `pa2kva(alloc_user_page(1, NULL) + PAGE_SIZE)` with exactly two arguments. Adding a third parameter fails to compile the given tree.

3) The suggested fix "allocate raw and zero at the call site" is a regression, not a cleanup. There are five call sites: mm.c:222 (swap-in, the only one that does not need zeroing), mm.c:229 (fresh demand-paged user page), mm.c:342 (shm_page_get, a pinned frame handed to multiple user processes), kernel/sched/sched.c:256 and init/main.c:99 (kernel stacks). Four of the five require a clean frame, and one of those four is in given code that cannot be edited to add the zeroing. Making zeroing opt-in trades a guaranteed invariant ("every frame this allocator hands out is clean") for a per-caller obligation, on an allocator that recycles frames between distinct user address spaces via selete_page()/write_to_sd(). That is precisely the change that would create a real cross-process data-leak bug.

4) The performance argument is off by orders of magnitude and misattributes the lock-hold cost. memset is a naive byte loop (/workspace/Project4-Virtual_Memory_Management/libs/string.c:10-17), so ~4096 stores — a few thousand to ~16k cycles. Its immediate neighbor sbi_sd_read is an ecall into M-mode firmware performing eight 512-byte SD block transfers; SD command/response plus transfer latency is milliseconds, several orders of magnitude larger. Worse for the claim: when this path also has to evict (alloc_user_page mm.c:60-65 calls selete_page() then write_to_sd()), a full sbi_sd_write of another page happens under the same lock. The "both harts serialised behind the global kernel lock" cost on the swap-in path is entirely SD I/O; removing the memset would not be measurable.

5) The memset is not even unambiguously dead there. sbi_sd_read's return status is discarded at mm.c:223. On a failed or partial transfer, the pre-zeroing is the only thing preventing the previous owner's frame contents from being mapped into the faulting user process at mm.c:233-234 with _PAGE_USER | _PAGE_READ. Unconditional zeroing in the allocator is a deliberate defensive invariant, not an oversight.

REFUTED — the finding rests on a pre-existing framework constant, an unreachable exhaustion scenario, and a factually wrong premise about clean pages.

1) The 256-slot limit is NOT new code. `git show HEAD:Project4-Virtual_Memory_Management/include/os/mm.h` line 86 already contains `#define DISK_PAGE_NUM 256`, the `disk_page_t` struct, and `extern disk_page_t disk_page[DISK_PAGE_NUM]` (plus `#define SWAP_BEGIN 2048` at line 54). The diff to /workspace/Project4-Virtual_Memory_Management/include/os/mm.h adds only the `alloc_page_helper`/`find_pte` declarations and the SHM_VA_*/USER_CODE_*/SD_BLOCK_* constants — it does not touch the swap table size. 256 slots is also exactly the SD region the framework reserved: SWAP_BEGIN=2048 blocks + 256*8 = 2048 blocks ends at block 4096. Using more slots than DISK_PAGE_NUM would write past that region; the new code correctly stays inside the given budget.

2) Assert-on-pool-exhaustion is the framework's own convention, in given code. `alloc_pgdir_page()` at /workspace/Project4-Virtual_Memory_Management/kernel/mm/mm.c:19-31 is unmodified pre-existing code and does the identical thing: linear scan then `assert(i != PGDIR_PAGE_NUM)`. "Fail the allocation instead" is not expressible here: `alloc_user_page`'s signature is fixed by the given header (`extern ptr_t alloc_user_page(uint8_t, PTE*)`, mm.h:94, no error convention), and `alloc_page_helper` must match the given `load_elf` callback type `uintptr_t (*prepare_page_for_va)(uintptr_t, uintptr_t)` (/workspace/Project4-Virtual_Memory_Management/include/os/elf.h:140-142), whose body at elf.h:170-181 dereferences the returned pointer unconditionally with no failure path. A "failing" return would turn a clean panic into a wild kernel memcpy.

3) The exhaustion is unreachable by roughly three orders of magnitude. A swap-out only occurs after the scan in alloc_user_page (mm.c:51-56) finds zero free frames, i.e. after all USER_PAGE_NUM = (0x5e000000-0x51000000)/4096 = 53248 frames (208 MiB) are simultaneously live; the 257th eviction needs 53248+257 live allocations. NUM_MAX_TASK is 16 (include/os/sched.h:39), each process costs one pinned kernel-stack frame (sched.c:243) plus its touched pages, and the heaviest provided workload, /workspace/Project4-Virtual_Memory_Management/test/swap.c, touches `4096*8` unsigned longs at 0x20000000 = 256 KiB = 64 frames. Sixteen concurrent copies is ~1100 frames. Under the provided tests selete_page/write_to_sd are never entered at all. Slots also cannot leak into the limit: alloc_page_helper releases the slot on swap-in (`disk_page[slot].valid = 0`, mm.c:216) and free_process_user_page releases the slots of _PAGE_SOFT leaves at exit (mm.c ~303-306).

4) The "clean pages burn slots" sub-claim is factually wrong for this code. Every mapping alloc_page_helper creates is stamped `_PAGE_PRESENT|_PAGE_READ|_PAGE_WRITE|_PAGE_EXEC|_PAGE_USER|_PAGE_ACCESSED|_PAGE_DIRTY` (mm.c:233-234), and shm_page_get does the same (mm.c:353-354). No page is ever clean, so a _PAGE_DIRTY test would filter exactly zero evictions. The ELF text pages init_page_table maps at mm.c:259-261 go through that same path and are writable — not read-only — and dropping/reloading them would require per-page file provenance that the given loader contract never records.

5) `assert(0)` in selete_page (mm.c:119) is likewise unreachable. Pinned frames are only kernel stacks (<=16, sched.c:243 / init/main.c:99) and shm frames (<=SHM_PAGE_NUM=100), i.e. at most ~116 of 53248 frames; and the 2*USER_PAGE_NUM bound guarantees a victim, since the first sweep clears every _PAGE_ACCESSED bit. Memory can never be full while leaving no evictable frame.

6) That do_exec's `free_page_num() < EXEC_MIN_FREE_PAGES` guard (sched.c:214) ignores disk_page[] is not a defect: swapping only begins once physical frames are gone, so a physical-frame admission check is the meaningful one at that point.

No concrete failure is demonstrable for any supported workload; the report describes a given design limit plus a speculative optimization.

REFUTED — the described window cannot open in this build: write_to_sd() is unreachable, so the claim is a theoretical ordering nit rather than a demonstrable defect.

1) The swap-out path is dead code in this configuration. write_to_sd() has exactly one caller, alloc_user_page() at /workspace/Project4-Virtual_Memory_Management/kernel/mm/mm.c:60-63, reached only after the linear scan over all USER_PAGE_NUM entries finds no free frame. USER_PAGE_NUM = (USER_MEM_END - USER_MEM_BEGIN)/PAGE_SIZE with the given, unmodified constants in /workspace/Project4-Virtual_Memory_Management/include/os/mm.h:50-51 (0x51000000..0x5e000000) = 53248 frames = 208 MB. The git diff of mm.h touches only lines 102+ (new prototypes and the SHM/USER_CODE/SD_BLOCK macros); the memory-layout constants are pre-existing context. Nothing in the tree can consume 53248 frames: NUM_MAX_TASK is 16 (/workspace/Project4-Virtual_Memory_Management/include/os/sched.h:39), the heaviest test /workspace/Project4-Virtual_Memory_Management/test/swap.c touches LENGTH = 4096*8 longs at 0x20000000 = 64 data pages, and each process costs ~5 code pages (USER_CODE_BEGIN..END) + stack pages + 1 pinned kernel-stack page. Worst case is roughly 1150 frames — 46x headroom. Pages are also returned on exit (free_process_user_page at kernel/sched/sched.c:432, kernel stack at sched.c:470 and init/main.c:211), so no accumulating leak closes that gap. selete_page()/write_to_sd() therefore never execute and the frame P is running out of on hart 1 is never chosen as a victim.

2) Even granting reachability, the failure needs an exact interleaving: hart 1 must store to that one victim frame during the few microseconds hart 0 spends inside sbi_sd_write(pa, 8 blocks, ...) (mm.c:134) and before clear_attribute(_PAGE_PRESENT) at mm.c:142. No shipped test can produce that deterministically.

3) The mechanical premises do check out, so this is a legitimate design remark rather than a fabrication — the kernel lock is released before sret (call unlock_kernel at arch/riscv/kernel/entry.S:157, spin_lock_release in kernel/sched/smp.c:35), both harts run user tasks (init/main.c:124-125 plus the set_satp in kernel/sched/sched.c:117), alloc_page_helper grants _PAGE_WRITE|_PAGE_DIRTY unconditionally (mm.c:233-234), and flush_tlb_all() really is a cross-hart shootdown (local_flush_tlb_all(); sbi_remote_sfence_vma(NULL, 0, -1) in arch/riscv/include/pgtable.h:28-32), so invalidate-then-shootdown-then-write would be the textbook-correct order. But "the code would be racy if the swap path ever ran" is not exhibitable here: with 208 MB of user memory and a 16-task, ~1150-frame ceiling, no execution of this kernel enters write_to_sd.

Relevant files: /workspace/Project4-Virtual_Memory_Management/kernel/mm/mm.c (lines 50-77, 95-149), /workspace/Project4-Virtual_Memory_Management/include/os/mm.h (lines 44-52, 70-77), /workspace/Project4-Virtual_Memory_Management/test/swap.c, /workspace/Project4-Virtual_Memory_Management/arch/riscv/include/pgtable.h.

REFUTED. (1) The keyless table is given, not new: `git show HEAD:Project4-Virtual_Memory_Management/include/os/mm.h` proves `#define SHM_PAGE_NUM 100` and `typedef struct shm_page{int count; uintptr_t pa;}` (lines 79-84) are unchanged framework code; the new diff to that header only adds SHM_VA_BEGIN/END, USER_CODE_*, and SD-block macros at line 102+. A fixed 100-entry descriptor array with no key field encodes the contract "key is the slot index, 0 <= key < 100". Under that contract `key % SHM_PAGE_NUM` is the identity map and is injective -- no two valid keys alias. Dropping the modulo would make key >= 100 an out-of-bounds write into shm_page[], so the modulo is strictly a safety guard, not the source of a bug. (2) No reachable trigger: grepping test/, tiny_libc/, include/ shows the sole shm user in the tree is /workspace/Project4-Virtual_Memory_Management/test/consensus.c with `#define SHMP_KEY 42` (all 9 consensus processes use it); test_shell.c passes no key and no key ever originates from user input. No program uses 142, 107, or any key >= 100, so the "two unrelated programs collide" scenario cannot occur. (3) The asserted harm is factually false: in /workspace/Project4-Virtual_Memory_Management/kernel/mm/mm.c, `page->count++` happens exactly once per successful mapping in shm_page_get (line 355), and count is decremented exactly once per unmap in shm_page_dt (line 385) and free_process_user_page (line 303), both guarded by `shm_page[i].count > 0 && shm_page[i].pa == pa`. count is therefore the additive total of live mappings across all processes and all keys landing in the slot, so count==0 implies zero live mappings and free_user_page(pa) can never run while another process is still attached -- there is no premature free and no use-after-free. Released slots also set pa = 0 while every lookup requires count > 0, so no stale-pa aliasing either. The only conceivable effect is data sharing between two out-of-contract keys, which no code in the tree can produce.

So with >=16 free frames guaranteed and 7 consumed, alloc_user_page never reaches its `i == USER_PAGE_NUM` branch, and selete_page() is never called from do_exec — the caller's argv/file_name pages cannot be evicted mid-syscall.
